h2. Section 5: Introduction to Styled Components

Beyond {{StyleSheet}} and inline styles, the React Native community widely uses CSS-in-JS libraries to create more dynamic, reusable, and themeable styling solutions. One of the most popular such libraries is {{styled-components}}. This section introduces {{styled-components}}, its core concepts, benefits, and how to start using it in your SpeedyMeds application.

h3. What are Styled Components?

{{styled-components}} allow you to write actual CSS code to style your components using tagged template literals. It brings the power of ES6 template literals and CSS together to create React components with styles attached directly to them. This approach results in components that are inherently styled, making your styling logic more colocated and component-centric.

*Key Benefits of Styled Components:*
# *Scoped Styles:* Styles are automatically scoped to the component, eliminating concerns about class name collisions or global style leakage.
# *Dynamic Styling with Props:* Easily adapt styles based on component props, leading to highly reusable and configurable components.
# *CSS Syntax:* You can use familiar CSS syntax (with some React Native specific considerations), which can be more intuitive for developers with a web background.
# *Theming:* Built-in support for theming allows you to define a consistent look and feel across your application and switch themes easily.
# *Automatic Vendor Prefixing (for web):* While less relevant for React Native, it showcases the library's robustness.
# *Better Readability (Subjective):* Some developers find that colocating styles with component definitions improves readability and maintainability.

h3. Installation

To use {{styled-components}} in your Expo React Native project, you need to install it.

First, install the library itself:

{code:language=bash}
h1. Using npm
npm install styled-components

h1. Or using yarn
yarn add styled-components
{code}

Since `styled-components` relies on TypeScript types for a better development experience, and if you are using TypeScript (as recommended in this course), you should also install its type definitions:

{code:language=bash}
h1. Using npm
npm install --save-dev @types/styled-components-react-native

h1. Or using yarn
yarn add --dev @types/styled-components-react-native
{code}

{note}
For React Native, you specifically import from `styled-components/native`.
As of `styled-components` v6 and later, the library is written in TypeScript and typically bundles its own type definitions. The separate `@types/styled-components-react-native` package might still be needed for older versions or specific project configurations, but always check the official `styled-components` documentation for the most up-to-date TypeScript integration instructions for the version you are using.
{note}
h3. Basic Usage

Let's create a simple styled button for our SpeedyMeds app.

{code:language=js}
import React from "react";
import { Text, TouchableOpacityProps } from "react-native";
import styled from "styled-components/native"; // Import from /native

// Define an interface for the props that StyledButtonContainer will accept for styling
/**
* Props for the StyledButtonContainer styled component.
* These props control the visual appearance of the button container.
* @param primary - Optional flag to indicate if the button should have primary styling.
* @param disabled - Optional flag to indicate if the button should appear disabled.
 */
interface StyledButtonContainerProps {
  primary?: boolean;
  disabled?: boolean;
}

// Define a styled TouchableOpacity component using the interface for its props
const StyledButtonContainer = styled.TouchableOpacity<StyledButtonContainerProps>`
  background-color: ${(props) => (props.primary ? "#007bff" : "#6c757d")};
  padding: 12px 20px;
  border-radius: 8px;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  margin-vertical: 10px; /* Example of a CSS-like property */

  /* Example of adapting styles based on a prop */
  opacity: ${(props) => (props.disabled ? 0.5 : 1)};
`;

// Define a styled Text component for the button label
const StyledButtonText = styled.Text`
  color: white;
  font-size: 16px;
  font-weight: bold;
`;

/**
* Props for the SpeedyButton component.
* Extends TouchableOpacityProps to accept all standard touchable opacity props.
* @param title - The text to display on the button.
* @param primary - Optional flag to render the button with primary styling.
* @param disabled - Optional flag to render the button in a disabled state (inherited by StyledButtonContainer).
 */
interface SpeedyButtonProps extends TouchableOpacityProps {
  title: string;
  primary?: boolean;
  // disabled is inherited from TouchableOpacityProps and also used by StyledButtonContainerProps
}

/**
* A custom, styled button component for the SpeedyMeds application.
* It utilizes styled-components for its container and text, and supports
* primary and disabled states through props.
* @param {SpeedyButtonProps} props - The props for the SpeedyButton.
* @returns {React.ReactElement} The SpeedyButton component.
 */
const SpeedyButton: React.FC<SpeedyButtonProps> = ({
  title,
  primary,
  disabled,
  ...rest
}) => {
  return (
    <StyledButtonContainer primary={primary} disabled={disabled} {...rest}>
      <StyledButtonText>{title}</StyledButtonText>
    </StyledButtonContainer>
  );
};

// Example usage in a screen
// import { View } from 'react-native';
// const ActionsScreen = () => (
//   <View style={{ padding: 20 }}>
//     <SpeedyButton title="Submit Prescription" primary />
//     <SpeedyButton title="Cancel Order" />
//     <SpeedyButton title="View Details" primary disabled />
//   </View>
// );

export default SpeedyButton;
{code}

*Explanation of the Example:*
# *Import:* We import `styled` from `styled-components/native`.
# *Creating Styled Components:*
*** `styled.TouchableOpacity` creates a new component that is a `TouchableOpacity` but with the specified styles applied. The styles are written inside backticks (`` ` ``) which are template literals.
*** `styled.Text` creates a styled `Text` component.
# *CSS-like Syntax:* Inside the template literal, you can write CSS-like properties. React Native compatible properties are used (e.g., `backgroundColor`, `borderRadius`, `marginVertical`). Notice `margin-vertical` is a valid way to write it here, though `marginVertical` also works.
# *Adapting Based on Props:*
*** The `background-color` of `StyledButtonContainer` changes based on the `primary` prop: `background-color: ${(props) => props.primary ? '#007bff' : '#6c757d'};`.
*** The `opacity` changes based on the `disabled` prop: `opacity: ${(props) => props.disabled ? 0.5 : 1};`.
*** This is a powerful feature where style rules can be functions that receive the component's props and return a style value.
# *Usage:* The `SpeedyButton` component then uses `StyledButtonContainer` and `StyledButtonText` just like regular React Native components, passing props like `primary` and `disabled` to control their appearance.

h3. Styling Any Component

You can wrap existing React Native components (or your custom components) to style them. To style a third-party component or a custom component you've created, you can pass it to the `styled()` function:

{code:language=js}
import React from "react";
import { View } from "react-native";
import styled from "styled-components/native";

// Assume MyCustomCard is a component you defined elsewhere
interface MyCustomCardProps {
  title: string;
  children?: React.ReactNode;
  // other props
}
const MyCustomCard: React.FC<MyCustomCardProps> = ({ title, children }) => {
  // ... card implementation ...
  return (
    <View>
      <Text>{title}</Text>
      {children}
    </View>
  );
};

const StyledCustomCard = styled(MyCustomCard)`
  margin: 10px;
  padding: 15px;
  background-color: #f8f9fa;
  border: 1px solid #dee2e6;
  border-radius: 5px;
  /* Additional styles specific to this usage of MyCustomCard */
  ${(props: { urgent?: boolean }) =>
    props.urgent &&
    `
    border-left-width: 5px;
    border-left-color: red;
  `}
`;

// Usage
// <StyledCustomCard title="Patient Details" />
// <StyledCustomCard title="Urgent Medication Alert" urgent />
{code}

h3. Extending Styles

You can extend styles from another styled component, similar to class inheritance in CSS.

{code:language=js}
const BaseButton = styled.TouchableOpacity`
  padding: 10px 15px;
  border-radius: 5px;
  align-items: center;
`;

const PrimaryButton = styled(BaseButton)`
  background-color: #007bff;
`;

const SecondaryButton = styled(BaseButton)`
  background-color: #6c757d;
`;

// const ButtonText = styled.Text`color: white;`;
// <PrimaryButton><ButtonText>Primary Action</ButtonText></PrimaryButton>
{code}

This allows you to create a base set of styles and then create variations easily.

bq. 🌐 *(Web Developers):*
> *Comparison:* Styled Components work almost identically in React and React Native. The main difference is the set of valid CSS properties (React Native uses a subset and its own specific properties like `elevation` for Android shadow) and the base elements you style (e.g., `styled.View` instead of `styled.div`).
> *Key Takeaway:* If you've used Styled Components on the web, you'll feel right at home. Just remember to import from `styled-components/native` and use React Native compatible style properties.

h3. Considerations
* *Performance:* Styled Components is generally performant. It intelligently injects styles and avoids unnecessary re-renders. However, very complex dynamic styles within frequently updated components could potentially have an impact. As always, profile if you encounter issues.
* *Bundle Size:* Adding any library increases your app's bundle size. Styled Components is a reasonably sized library, but it's a factor to consider.
* *Learning Curve:* While CSS syntax is familiar, the concept of tagged template literals and function-based styles might take a little getting used to for those new to these JavaScript features.

Styled Components offer a powerful and expressive way to handle styling in React Native, particularly for applications with dynamic styling needs or those benefiting from a theming system. We will explore theming with Styled Components in the next section.
